q: Which statement about a redox reaction is correct?
o: Oxidation takes place without any reduction
Reduction always happens before oxidation is complete
Only non-metals take part in it
Oxidation and reduction take place at the same time
x: Electrons lost by one species must be gained by another, so oxidation and reduction always occur together. That is why the reaction is called redox.

q: In terms of electrons, oxidation is defined as:
o: Loss of electrons
Gain of electrons
Sharing of electrons
Gain of protons
x: Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons. Gaining protons has nothing to do with this definition.

q: Which of the following is NOT a redox reaction?
o: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O
x: In the neutralisation, Na stays +1, O −2, H +1 and Cl −1, so no oxidation number changes. In the other three, a free element becomes combined, so oxidation numbers change.

q: In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, electrons are transferred:
o: From zinc atoms to copper(II) ions
From copper(II) ions to zinc atoms
From zinc atoms to the sulphate ions
From water molecules to zinc atoms
x: Zn loses 2 electrons to become Zn²⁺ (oxidation) and Cu²⁺ gains them to become Cu (reduction). Sulphate ions are spectators.

q: In any balanced redox reaction, the total number of electrons lost by the reducing agent is:
o: Always greater than the number gained by the oxidising agent
Equal to the total number gained by the oxidising agent
Always less than the number gained by the oxidising agent
Unrelated to the number gained by the oxidising agent
x: Electrons cannot be created or destroyed, so those lost in oxidation must equal those gained in reduction. This is the basis for balancing redox equations.

q: Which change is an oxidation?
o: CuO → Cu
Cl₂ → Cl⁻
Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺
H₂S → S
x: H₂S losing hydrogen to form S is oxidation; sulphur goes from −2 to 0. The other three are reductions: loss of oxygen, gain of an electron, and a fall in charge.

q: In Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O, what happens to chlorine?
o: It is both oxidised (to +1) and reduced (to −1)
It is only oxidised, from 0 to +1
It is only reduced, from 0 to −1
It is neither oxidised nor reduced
x: Chlorine starts at 0. In NaCl it is −1 (reduced) and in NaClO it is +1 (oxidised). A reaction in which one element is both oxidised and reduced is called disproportionation.

q: Which of the following decomposition reactions is a redox reaction?
o: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
NH₄Cl → NH₃ + HCl
2HgO → 2Hg + O₂
Cu(OH)₂ → CuO + H₂O
x: In 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂, mercury goes from +2 to 0 and oxygen from −2 to 0. In the other three no oxidation number changes.

q: For the reaction Mg + Cl₂ → MgCl₂, the oxidation half-reaction is:
o: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻
Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg
2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻
x: Magnesium loses two electrons, so its half-reaction is the oxidation: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻. Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ is the reduction half-reaction.

q: How many electrons are transferred in the reaction 2Fe³⁺ + Sn²⁺ → 2Fe²⁺ + Sn⁴⁺ as written?
x: Sn²⁺ → Sn⁴⁺ loses 2 electrons; each Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺ gains 1, and there are 2 Fe³⁺. So 2 electrons are transferred in total.

q: In terms of oxidation number, oxidation is:
o: A decrease in the oxidation number of an atom
No change in the oxidation number of an atom
An increase in the oxidation number of an atom
A change of oxidation number to zero
x: Losing electrons makes an atom more positive, so oxidation is an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is a decrease.

q: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in H₂SO₄?
What is the oxidation number of manganese in KMnO₄?
x: (+1) + x + 4(−2) = 0, so x = +7. +2 is manganese in Mn²⁺ and +4 in MnO₂.

q: What is the oxidation number of chromium in K₂Cr₂O₇?
x: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0, so 2x = 12 and x = +6. +12 is the total for both Cr atoms, not each.

q: In which compound does oxygen have a positive oxidation number?
o: H₂O₂
Na₂O
H₂O
OF₂
x: Fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen and is always −1, so in OF₂ oxygen is +2. In H₂O₂ oxygen is −1, and in Na₂O and H₂O it is −2.

q: What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
x: x + 4(+1) = +1 (the charge on the ion), so x = −3. Ignoring the charge and setting the sum to zero gives −4.

q: What is the oxidation number of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH?
x: In metal hydrides hydrogen is bonded to a less electronegative metal, so it takes −1. Sodium is +1, giving a total of zero.

q: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in the thiosulphate ion, S₂O₃²⁻ (taking both S atoms as equal)?
x: 2x + 3(−2) = −2, so 2x = 4 and x = +2. +2.5 is the average value in the tetrathionate ion S₄O₆²⁻.

q: The oxidation number of each atom in O₂, P₄ and S₈ is:
o: +2, +4 and +8 respectively
−2 in all three
Equal to its group number
x: An element in its free, uncombined state always has oxidation number zero, whatever the size of its molecule.

q: When MnO₄⁻ is converted to Mn²⁺ in acidic solution, manganese is:
o: Reduced, as its oxidation number falls from +7 to +2
Oxidised, as its oxidation number rises from +2 to +7
Reduced, as its oxidation number falls from +6 to +2
Oxidised, as its oxidation number rises from +7 to +8
x: In MnO₄⁻, x + 4(−2) = −1 gives x = +7. Going to Mn²⁺ is a fall in oxidation number, which is reduction (a gain of 5 electrons).

q: An oxidising agent is a substance that:
o: Loses electrons and is itself oxidised
Gains electrons and is itself reduced
Gains protons and is itself oxidised
Neither gains nor loses electrons
x: An oxidising agent oxidises something else by taking its electrons, so it is itself reduced. A reducing agent gives electrons and is itself oxidised.

q: In the reaction Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, the reducing agent is:
o: CuSO₄
ZnSO₄
Zn
Cu
x: Zinc goes from 0 to +2, so it loses electrons and is oxidised; this makes it the reducing agent. Cu²⁺ in CuSO₄ is the oxidising agent.

q: In MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O, the oxidising agent is:
o: HCl
MnCl₂
Cl₂
MnO₂
x: Manganese falls from +4 in MnO₂ to +2 in MnCl₂, so MnO₂ is reduced and is the oxidising agent. Chlorine rises from −1 to 0, so HCl is the reducing agent.

q: In 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O, which statement is correct?
o: SO₂ is oxidised and H₂S is the oxidising agent
Both H₂S and SO₂ are oxidised
H₂S is oxidised and SO₂ is the oxidising agent
Sulphur does not change its oxidation number
x: Sulphur in H₂S goes from −2 to 0 (oxidised) and in SO₂ from +4 to 0 (reduced). So SO₂ is the oxidising agent and H₂S the reducing agent.

q: In Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O, which statement is correct?
o: Each Cr atom gains 6 electrons, and Fe²⁺ is reduced
Each Cr atom gains 3 electrons, and Fe²⁺ is oxidised
Each Cr atom loses 3 electrons, and Fe²⁺ is reduced
H⁺ is reduced to H₂, and Fe²⁺ is oxidised
x: Cr goes from +6 to +3, gaining 3 electrons per atom (6 for the two Cr). The 6 Fe²⁺ each lose one electron to become Fe³⁺, so they are oxidised. H⁺ is unchanged at +1.

q: In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, which species is reduced?
o: Na, because its oxidation number falls from +1 to 0
Na, because its oxidation number rises from 0 to +1
Cl₂, because its oxidation number falls from 0 to −1
Cl₂, because its oxidation number rises from 0 to +1
x: Chlorine gains electrons and goes from 0 to −1, which is reduction. Sodium goes from 0 to +1, which is oxidation.

q: Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂. Which species is oxidised?
o: Cl₂
I⁻
K⁺
Cl⁻
x: Iodide ions go from −1 to 0 in I₂, so they are oxidised. Cl₂ is reduced to Cl⁻, and K⁺ is a spectator ion.

q: Hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂, can act both as an oxidising agent and as a reducing agent because:
o: Hydrogen in it is −1, so it can rise to +1
Oxygen in it is already at its lowest value, −2
It contains no element that can change oxidation number
Oxygen in it is −1, so it can fall to −2 or rise to 0
x: Oxygen in H₂O₂ is −1, in between −2 (in H₂O) and 0 (in O₂). It can be reduced to −2 or oxidised to 0, so H₂O₂ can do both jobs.

q: In 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O, the nitrogen atoms that are reduced change their oxidation number from:
x: N in HNO₃ is +5 and in NO is +2. Only 2 of the 8 nitrogen atoms are reduced; the other 6 stay at +5 in the nitrate ions of Cu(NO₃)₂.

q: In the blast furnace reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, the reducing agent is:
o: Fe₂O₃, as iron falls from +3 to 0
CO, as carbon rises from +2 to +4
CO₂, as carbon falls from +4 to +2
Fe, as iron rises from 0 to +3
x: Carbon in CO (+2) is oxidised to +4 in CO₂, so CO gives electrons and is the reducing agent. Fe₂O₃ is reduced and is the oxidising agent.

q: Which sulphur species can act ONLY as a reducing agent?
o: H₂S
SO₂
S
H₂SO₄
x: Sulphur in H₂S is −2, its lowest oxidation state, so it can only be oxidised. In H₂SO₄ (+6) it can only be reduced; SO₂ (+4) and S (0) can act either way.

q: In any electrochemical cell, the anode is the electrode at which:
o: Reduction takes place
Oxidation takes place
No reaction takes place
Metal is always deposited
x: Oxidation always occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode, in both galvanic and electrolytic cells.

q: In a galvanic cell such as the Daniell cell, the cathode is:
o: The positive electrode, where reduction takes place
The negative electrode, where reduction takes place
The positive electrode, where oxidation takes place
The negative electrode, where oxidation takes place
x: In a galvanic cell electrons arrive at the cathode, where Cu²⁺ is reduced; this electrode is positive. In an electrolytic cell the cathode is the negative electrode, but reduction still occurs there.

q: In an electrolytic cell, the anode is:
o: Connected to the negative terminal of the battery, and oxidation occurs there
Connected to the positive terminal of the battery, and reduction occurs there
Connected to the negative terminal of the battery, and reduction occurs there
Connected to the positive terminal of the battery, and oxidation occurs there
x: In electrolysis the anode is joined to the positive terminal, so it attracts anions, which lose electrons (oxidation). The cathode is negative and reduction occurs there.

q: In the Daniell cell (Zn in ZnSO₄, Cu in CuSO₄), electrons flow through the external wire:
o: From the copper electrode to the zinc electrode
Through the salt bridge from zinc to copper
From the zinc electrode to the copper electrode
In both directions equally
x: Zinc is oxidised at the anode and releases electrons, which travel through the wire to the copper cathode where Cu²⁺ is reduced. Ions, not electrons, move through the salt bridge.

q: Electrode potential is the:
o: Current that flows through an electrolyte during electrolysis
Mass of metal deposited on an electrode
Potential difference set up between a metal and a solution of its own ions
Energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom
x: When a metal dips into a solution of its ions, an equilibrium is set up and a potential difference develops between them; this is the electrode potential. The last option describes ionisation energy.

q: The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) consists of:
o: A copper rod dipped in 1 mol dm⁻³ CuSO₄, with H₂ gas bubbled over it
Platinum in 0.1 mol dm⁻³ HCl, with O₂ gas bubbled over it
Platinum coated with platinum black in 1 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, with H₂ gas bubbled over it at standard pressure
A zinc rod dipped in 1 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄
x: The SHE is a platinised platinum electrode in a 1 mol dm⁻³ H⁺ solution with pure hydrogen at standard pressure and 25 °C. The other set-ups lack H⁺ at unit concentration or hydrogen gas.

q: By convention, the standard electrode potential of the standard hydrogen electrode is taken as:
x: The SHE is the reference electrode and is assigned 0.00 V. −0.76 V and +0.34 V are the standard potentials of the zinc and copper electrodes.

q: Platinum is used as the metal in the standard hydrogen electrode because it:
o: Reacts with H⁺ ions to produce hydrogen gas
Is inert and conducts electrons, and its platinum black coating adsorbs hydrogen
Has the most negative electrode potential of all metals
Is oxidised to Pt²⁺ ions, which supply the electrons
x: Platinum takes no part in the reaction; it only provides a conducting surface. The finely divided platinum black gives a large surface that adsorbs hydrogen so the H₂/H⁺ equilibrium is set up quickly.

q: The function of the salt bridge in a galvanic cell is to:
o: Carry electrons from the anode to the cathode
Supply the metal ions that are deposited at the cathode
Complete the circuit and keep both solutions electrically neutral
Prevent any reaction from taking place at the anode
x: Ions move through the salt bridge to balance the charge building up in each half-cell, which completes the circuit. Electrons travel through the external wire, not the bridge.

q: Why is the potential of an electrode always measured by connecting it to a standard hydrogen electrode?
o: The SHE supplies the electrons needed by every electrode
Hydrogen is the most reactive element, so it gives the largest reading
The potential of a single electrode cannot be measured on its own; only a difference between two electrodes can
The SHE makes the electrode react faster
x: A voltmeter measures only the potential difference between two electrodes. So a reference electrode with an agreed value of 0.00 V, the SHE, is used and the measured cell voltage gives the electrode's potential.

q: The standard electrode potential (E°) of an electrode is its potential measured against the SHE with:
o: 1 mol dm⁻³ ion concentration at 25 °C (gases at standard pressure)
0.1 mol dm⁻³ ion concentration at 0 °C
Any ion concentration at room temperature
1 mol dm⁻³ ion concentration at 100 °C
x: Standard conditions are 1 mol dm⁻³ for ions, 298 K (25 °C) and standard pressure for any gas, with the electrode connected to the SHE.

q: E° for Zn²⁺/Zn is −0.76 V and for Cu²⁺/Cu is +0.34 V. Which statement is correct?
o: Zinc is a stronger reducing agent than copper
Copper is a stronger reducing agent than zinc
Zn²⁺ is a stronger oxidising agent than Cu²⁺
Zinc and copper are equally good reducing agents
x: A more negative E° means the metal loses electrons more easily, so zinc is the stronger reducing agent. Correspondingly, Cu²⁺ is the stronger oxidising agent.

q: Standard electrode potentials: Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V, Mg²⁺/Mg −2.37 V, Hg²⁺/Hg +0.85 V. Which metal liberates hydrogen from dilute HCl?
o: Copper
Silver
Magnesium
Mercury
x: Metals with a negative E° (below hydrogen at 0.00 V) can reduce H⁺ to H₂. Only magnesium has a negative value; copper, silver and mercury have positive values and do not react.

q: E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V and E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V. What is the standard emf of the Daniell cell?
x: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = +0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V. Simply adding the two values gives −0.42 V, a common mistake.

q: Lithium has one of the most negative standard electrode potentials. This means lithium:
o: Is a very strong oxidising agent
Is a very strong reducing agent and is very easily oxidised
Cannot lose electrons easily
Does not react with water
x: The more negative the E°, the greater the tendency to lose electrons. Lithium is therefore oxidised very easily and is a very powerful reducing agent.

q: Fluorine has the most positive standard electrode potential (F₂/F⁻). This means fluorine is:
o: The strongest reducing agent
The strongest oxidising agent
Not able to gain electrons
Less reactive than iodine
x: A very positive E° means a very strong tendency to gain electrons, i.e. to be reduced. So F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent, while F⁻ is a very weak reducing agent.

q: A copper strip is placed in ZnSO₄ solution. E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V. What happens?
o: No reaction, because copper is a weaker reducing agent than zinc
Zinc is deposited on the copper
Copper dissolves and zinc is deposited
Hydrogen gas is given off
x: Copper's E° is more positive, so it cannot reduce Zn²⁺ ions. The reverse reaction does occur: zinc placed in CuSO₄ solution displaces copper.

q: E° values: Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V. Which metal can reduce Fe²⁺ ions to iron?
o: Copper
Zinc
Silver
Copper and silver, but not zinc
x: A metal can reduce Fe²⁺ only if its E° is more negative than −0.44 V. Only zinc (−0.76 V) qualifies; copper and silver have more positive values.

q: E° of the Zn²⁺/Zn electrode is −0.76 V. When this electrode is connected to the SHE, the zinc electrode acts as the:
o: Anode, and electrons flow from zinc to the SHE
Cathode, and electrons flow from the SHE to zinc
Cathode, and zinc ions are reduced
Anode, and hydrogen is evolved at the zinc
x: The negative sign means zinc has a greater tendency than hydrogen to be oxidised. So zinc is the anode, and electrons flow from it to the SHE, where H⁺ is reduced.

q: E° values: Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V, Br₂/Br⁻ +1.09 V, I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V. Which reaction takes place?
o: I₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2I⁻ + Br₂
Br₂ + 2Cl⁻ → 2Br⁻ + Cl₂
I₂ + 2Cl⁻ → 2I⁻ + Cl₂
Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂
x: A halogen with a more positive E° is a stronger oxidising agent and displaces the halide of a less positive one. Cl₂ (+1.36 V) can oxidise Br⁻, but I₂ cannot oxidise Br⁻ or Cl⁻.
